content: If the patient is HIV-infected, provide the appropriate treatment as outlined in guidelines G6 and G9. In cases of heavy vaginal bleeding, palpate the uterus. If the uterus is not firm, perform fundal massage to encourage contraction and expel any clots (refer to guideline B6). If a sanitary pad becomes soaked in less than five minutes, manage the situation as per guideline B5. If the bleeding originates from a perineal tear, repair the tear or refer the patient to a hospital (see guideline B17). If she is unable to urinate or her bladder is full (indicated by swelling over the lower abdomen) and she is uncomfortable, assist her by gently pouring water over the vulva. Avoid catheterization unless absolutely necessary. Review the patient’s medical records and administer any due treatments or prophylaxis. Provide advice on postpartum care and nutrition (refer to guideline D26). Educate the mother on when to seek medical care (see guideline D28). Offer counseling on birth spacing and family planning methods (refer to guideline D27). Conduct a repeat examination of the mother before discharge, following the postpartum assessment guidelines (D21). If the mother desires tubal ligation or an intrauterine device (IUD), make the necessary arrangements before discharge. After an uncomplicated vaginal birth in a healthcare facility, both the mother and newborn should remain under observation for at least 24 hours. Use the provided chart to examine the mother one hour after delivery or later, and again before discharge. For newborn examinations, refer to guidelines J2–J8. During the postpartum assessment, check the medical record for the following: bleeding exceeding 250 mL, completeness of the placenta and membranes, complications during delivery or postpartum, and any special treatment needs. Assess whether the mother requires tubal ligation or an IUD. Ask the mother how she is feeling, whether she has any pain or concerns, and inquire about the baby’s condition. Examine the perineum for tears, redness, swelling, or pus drainage. Discuss birth spacing and family planning options (D27). Advise her on when to seek care and schedule the next routine postpartum visit (D28). Reassess her condition before discharge (D21). Continue any treatments initiated earlier. If tubal ligation is desired, refer her to a hospital within seven days of delivery. If an IUD is desired, refer her to appropriate services within 48 hours. In cases of heavy bleeding (e.g., more than one pad soaked in five minutes) or if the uterus is not firm and round, refer to guideline B5 for treatment and urgently transfer the patient to a hospital (B17). If the mother has a fever (temperature >38°C), assess the time since membrane rupture, abdominal pain, and chills. If the fever persists, check for abnormal vaginal discharge, fetal heart rate abnormalities, and lower abdominal tenderness. If uterine or fetal infection is suspected, initiate IV fluids (B9), administer appropriate antibiotics (B15), and, if the baby and placenta have been delivered, give oxytocin (10 IU IM, B10). Urgently refer the woman to a hospital (B17) and assess the newborn for signs of infection (J2–J8). For third-degree perineal tears extending to the anus or rectum, urgently refer the woman to a hospital (B15). For smaller perineal tears or episiotomies, repair the tear if bleeding persists (B12). For severe pre-eclampsia, administer magnesium sulfate (B13) and urgently refer the patient to a hospital if in early labor or postpartum (B17). For severe anemia (Hb <7 g/dL), urgently refer the patient to a hospital (B17). For moderate anemia (Hb 7–11 g/dL), provide a double dose of iron for three months and follow up in four weeks. For no anemia, provide iron/folate supplementation for three months (F3). Assist her in re-establishing breastfeeding as soon as possible (K2–K3). If the baby is stillborn or has died, provide supportive care by informing the parents promptly, allowing them to hold the baby if culturally appropriate, and discussing the events leading to the death. Offer counseling on family planning and breast care (D27, K8). Vitamin A supplementation is not recommended for postpartum women. Encourage the use of insecticide-treated bed nets to prevent malaria. Counsel on postpartum care, nutrition, breastfeeding, safer sex practices, and family planning. Record all treatments and findings in the patient’s medical record. For family planning, explain that a woman can become pregnant as early as four weeks postpartum if not exclusively breastfeeding. Discuss the importance of waiting at least two years before attempting another pregnancy for the health of both mother and baby. Provide information on contraceptive options, including condoms, progestogen-only methods, IUDs, and sterilization. For breastfeeding women, emphasize the lactational amenorrhea method (LAM) as a temporary contraceptive option if specific criteria are met. Advise the mother to return for routine postpartum visits within 24 hours, on day three, and between days seven and 14 after delivery. Educate her on danger signs requiring immediate medical attention, such as heavy vaginal bleeding, convulsions, difficulty breathing, fever with weakness, severe abdominal pain, calf pain or swelling, foul-smelling lochia, or severe depression. Discuss emergency preparedness, including transportation, costs, and community support. Provide immediate postpartum care for the mother and newborn, including breastfeeding support, examination, and immunization.
